blend-sky.start: Start with Sky blue along the top edge of the canvas, from the left edge right across to the right edge.
blend-sky.strokes: Pull long side-to-side strokes across the whole width and work down. Without rinsing, pick up Warm gold, paint below the blue, then stroke back up over the join several times while it's wet.
blend-sky.inside: Keep the blue strongest in the upper left of the sky. Let the gold take over lower down, warmest toward the right edge, where the sun is setting behind the hills.
blend-sky.leave: Stop the sky about 3 1/2 in from the top edge, with a soft, wavy lower edge. Leave the canvas under it bare white, because the hills will cover it.
blend-sky.stop: You have a smooth band of sky, blue at the top melting into gold, with no hard line between them. If a line shows, add a little more gold at the join and blend again.

lay-clouds.first: Let the sky dry completely first, or the gold will smear into the blue.
lay-clouds.start: Start high in the sky at the right edge with long streaks. Here the cloud streaks reach up to the top edge.
lay-clouds.strokes: Skim the nearly dry brush side to side in light, flat strokes, keeping the bottom of each streak flat. Build them up in a few light passes.
lay-clouds.inside: Put most of it on the right side in long streaks. Run a broken band across the whole width low in the sky, just above its wavy edge, and dab a few small puffs higher up in the middle.
lay-clouds.leave: Leave plenty of blue showing in the upper left of the sky and between the streaks. Keep the bare canvas under the sky clean.
lay-clouds.stop: You have feathery gold streaks with blue showing through their edges, never a solid block. If one goes on solid, the brush was too loaded: wipe it on a rag before your next stroke.

light-clouds.first: Let the gold cloud streaks from step 2 dry first.
light-clouds.start: Start at the left edge, on the upper edge of the low gold band, about 2 1/2 in from the top edge.
light-clouds.strokes: Skim the dry brush lightly side to side along the upper edge of each streak, in short, broken passes.
light-clouds.inside: The cream goes only on the tops of the streaks, where the low sun catches them. Most of it goes on the left side, along the low band and on the small puffs.
light-clouds.leave: Leave the warm gold showing under each cream top, and the blue showing between the streaks.
light-clouds.stop: Each streak has a pale, feathery top with gold beneath it. The sky is finished.

lay-hillside.first: The violet hills and the loch must be dry.
lay-hillside.start: Start at the left edge, about 3 1/2 in from the top edge, just under the violet hills.
lay-hillside.strokes: Pull long left-to-right strokes that slope gently down toward the right edge, following the roll of the land.
lay-hillside.inside: Lay the green in long, sloping bands all the way down to the bottom edge. Where the cow will stand, fill one solid block with a flat coat; its left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge.
lay-hillside.leave: Leave a stripe of violet between each pair of bands, about as wide as a band, because the dark patches go there next. Keep the loch and the far hills clean.
lay-hillside.stop: From under the hills to the bottom edge, the land is striped olive and violet, with one flat green block in the middle. Don't cover all the violet.

patch-hillside.first: Let the olive-green bands from step 7 dry first.
patch-hillside.start: Start along the top of the hillside at the left edge, about 3 1/4 in from the top edge, just under the violet hills.
patch-hillside.strokes: Pull short, level strokes left and right, tilting them down toward the right edge with the slope of the land.
patch-hillside.inside: Fill the violet stripes between the olive bands. Keep the patches small and close together near the hills and bigger toward the bottom edge. Lay one long dark band along the top of the hillside, out to the loch.
patch-hillside.leave: Leave the olive bands showing between the dark streaks, and don't touch the flat block for the cow.
patch-hillside.stop: No violet shows on the hillside anymore. It rolls back in stripes of olive and deep green, bolder in front.

lay-meadow.first: Let the hillside from steps 7 and 8 dry first.
lay-meadow.start: Start at the left edge, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge, at the top of the meadow.
lay-meadow.strokes: Load both greens and make short X strokes that cross each other, working down to the bottom edge. Let the strokes at the meadow's top point up like grass tips.
lay-meadow.inside: Use more Olive green low down and more Yellow-green along the top and toward the right edge, where the sun lights the grass.
lay-meadow.leave: Don't touch the flat block for the cow, and leave a few small gaps where the hillside stripes peek through.
lay-meadow.stop: The lower canvas is a soft, criss-cross green meadow with a ragged top. Don't smooth it flat: the texture stays.

highland-cow.note: Two places where the pictures and the plan disagree: for step 1 the plan runs the gold down to the bottom edge, but the picture stops the sky about 3 1/2 in from the top. For step 3 the plan puts more cream on the right toward the sun, but the change and the facts put most of it on the left.

light-ledge.first: Let the darker brown from step 8 dry fully, or the dry brush will drag it into mud.
light-ledge.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, at the top of the sunlit patches, about 8 1/2 in from the top edge, just inside the wooden ledge.
light-ledge.strokes: With only the tip loaded and no water, skim light strokes from the left edge toward the window light's far end, following the slant of each patch. Build it in several light passes.
light-ledge.inside: The light falls through the window, so the patches glow strongest near the left edge and thin to small broken dabs where they stop, about 9 1/2 in from the left edge.
light-ledge.leave: Leave the thin dark bars from step 8 between the patches, the shadows of the window frame, and the dark front strip of the ledge.
light-ledge.stop: Stop at soft, see-through peachy patches with wood showing through, never solid. If one goes solid, let it dry and dry-brush brown back over part of it.

sleeping-cat.note: The picture leaves part of the patches, from about 4 1/4 in from the left edge, as one flat coat for the blanket to cover. I couldn't fit that in without going over the word limits.

variant.note: Step 7 puts a flat olive block on the canvas where the cow will go. It is exactly the blotch-before-its-step the owner marks down, and it stays there as a hard, unbrushlike shape through steps 8 and 9. In step 8 the block also changes from a ragged patch with violet holes to a clean solid silhouette, though the words say not to touch it. From step 10 on it matches B: sensible order, but step 14 turns the whole shaded cow into a finished shaggy coat in one go.

baseline.note: There is no placeholder. The sky gold covers the whole canvas in step 1, as the words say, and the hillside and meadow are laid in plainly before the cow arrives, so nothing shows early. Its weak points are the ones both lessons share. Step 4 goes from sky to full banded violet hills, step 14 goes from shaded cow to a full lock-by-lock coat, and step 16's picture reshapes the chin and jaw beyond 'a 1 in nose'. Step 5's change is also barely visible.

ab.note: From step 10 on the two lessons are nearly identical, so the choice rests on steps 1 and 7 to 9. There A has a flat cow-shaped block sitting in the land for three steps and changing shape unasked, and B has nothing like it. That is one of the owner's named faults, so B is the clear pick, though the margin is limited to that one stretch.

baseline.note: The background builds the way a real painting does: a sky over the whole canvas, violet underlayer, olive bands, dark fills, then the meadow, and nothing turns up early. Step 8 is a big jump: one Deep green ends up as a varied, finished-looking hillside plus a new dark ridge by the loch. Step 10 points to an outline picture the painter doesn't have, and step 21's glowing rim is a lot to get in one pass.

variant.note: Steps 7 to 9 carry a flat, hard-edged olive blob where the cow will stand, which is the 'ghost before its step' the owner marks down. Step 7 asks for it with no shape, only a left-edge distance. It changes from a ragged patch in step 7 to a clean cow silhouette in step 8, though step 8 says not to touch it, and step 10's cow doesn't match it anyway. The sky band over bare white in steps 1 to 3 is sensible, and from step 10 on B is the same as A.

ab.note: From step 10 on the two lessons are the same, so the choice rests on steps 1 to 9, and B's flat cow-shaped placeholder is the kind of flaw the owner has sunk lessons for. A's weak spots (the step 8 jump, the missing outline reference) are shared or milder. Confidence: clear, though not overwhelming, since most of the lesson is identical.

variant.note: Steps 1-10 and 12-20 are the same pictures and words as B, so the shared faults apply here too. Step 14 leaves hard-edged flat gray paw and chest shapes as ghosts before step 15. It also turns a flat silhouette into a nearly modelled kitten in one go. Step 11 jumps from flat yellow to finished chunky knit and reshapes the blanket's rolls. On top of that, step 9 shows a dark blob in the middle of the sunlit patch, plus a smaller one to its right; no word or paint covers either, and a beginner would wonder what they did wrong.

baseline.note: B has the same shared faults as A. Step 14 shows ghost paw and chest patches and a big jump to a shaded kitten. Step 11 goes from flat to finished knit. Step 6 asks for Wall blue only but shows warm peach light on the sill, and a dark ghost sits at the right edge of the wall from step 2 on. Unlike A, step 9 here shows clean, broken slanting bands of light that match its simpler words.

ab.note: The two lessons are identical except for step 9. There A has an unexplained dark blotch on the ledge, a mark no brush in the step makes, and B does not. The blanket covers the blotch at step 10, and both lessons share the bigger problems at steps 11 and 14, so the edge is slight, close to a toss-up.

baseline.note: The pictures read as a real painting building up from back to front, and most steps match their words and paints. Step 14 is the biggest problem. It asks only for Dark gray shading, but the picture also shows the head structure, ear forms and muzzle, plus hard-edged flat gray placeholders where the paws and chest will go, which no brush makes. Two smaller problems: step 8's sunlit patches have ragged, pixel-like edges, and step 18's 'Light gray' (#6e686c) is darker than the base gray, while the picture shows almost no change.

variant.note: B is the same as A in every step but 9, so it has the same step 14, 8 and 18 problems. In step 9 the picture puts a dark, solid blob in the middle of the sunlit patch (plus a smaller speck to the right). The words don't mention it, and they say the patches should be soft, see-through and 'never solid', so a painter comparing would be confused. The new step 9 words are clearer about where the light fades, but they give inch distances without giving the canvas size.

ab.note: Only step 9 differs between the two. A's step 9 is clean, while B's shows a stray dark blotch that its words don't ask for, which is one of the owner's listed faults. The blob is covered by the blanket in step 10, so the edge is real but small. My preference for A is slight, close to a toss-up.

variant.note: The landscape builds up believably: a sky band, a violet underlayer, olive bands with gaps, dark fills, then the meadow. Its sky steps match the words, leaving bare white below the 3 1/2 in line. Step 14 jumps from a soft-shaded cow to fully separated multi-tone locks using one Ginger paint. Step 16 names only a nose, but the head and fringe are reshaped. Step 22's horns turn tan along their whole length, not just a skimmed outer curve, and step 3's cream tops barely show.

baseline.note: From step 4 on, every picture and every word is the same as A, so it shares A's jumps at 14, 16 and 22. The only difference is steps 1-3: the whole canvas is covered in blue-to-gold, and its words match. The lower gold carries more deliberate orange cloud streaks than 'a few soft streaks' suggests, but the hills cover all of it in step 4, so it neither helps nor hurts.

ab-open.note: The two lessons differ only in whether step 1 leaves the canvas below the sky bare or covers it with gold. The hills cover that area in step 4 either way, and from there the pictures are identical. A's bare canvas is slightly tidier and B's full coverage is slightly more forgiving; neither is a real preference. Confidence that there is no real difference: clear.

baseline.note: From step 4 on this is the same lesson as B, picture for picture. Step 7's green patches have hard, pixel-stair edges no brush makes. Step 8 does far more than 'fill the purple stripes': the whole hillside turns into bushy dark blobs. Step 10 points to an outline 'on the Where picture' that doesn't exist, and step 5's change is almost invisible. The only difference from B is steps 1-3: here the gold sky with orange streaks fills the whole canvas, and step 4's violet then buries all of it, which is wasted work but doesn't mislead.

variant.note: Steps 4-22 match A exactly, with the same hard-edged step 7 patches, the step 8 hillside jump beyond its words, the missing outline in step 10 and the near-invisible step 5. Steps 1-3 paint only a sky band with a wavy edge over bare white, and the words and pictures agree on where it stops. That is a little more sensible than A's full-canvas gold, but it changes nothing a painter would notice by the end.

ab-open.note: The two lessons are the same from step 4 to the finish. They differ only in whether the sky gold runs to the bottom edge (A) or stops at a band over white canvas (B), and step 4 covers either way. B's sky start is marginally tidier, but that is a small edge, not a preference: a toss-up.

blend-sky.start: Start at the sky's upper left corner with Sky blue, right along the top edge of the canvas.
blend-sky.strokes: Stroke side to side across the full width. Without rinsing, pick up Warm gold and paint the band under the blue. Then stroke back up over the join several times while both are wet.
blend-sky.inside: Blue fills the top of the sky. The gold sits lower down and is strongest toward the right edge of the canvas, where the low sun is.
blend-sky.leave: Stop about 3 1/4 in from the top edge and leave the rest of the canvas white. The hills cover that ragged bottom edge later.
blend-sky.stop: A smooth band of sky runs across the top of the canvas, clear blue melting into gold. If you see a hard line where the colors meet, add more gold at the join and blend again.

lay-clouds.first: Let the sky dry completely, or the dry brush will smear it.
lay-clouds.start: Start near the sky's upper right corner with just the tip of the brush in Warm gold.
lay-clouds.strokes: Skim the brush lightly left and right in long, flat strokes, so each streak has a flat bottom and broken, feathery edges. Build it up in several light passes.
lay-clouds.inside: Most of the gold goes on the right half of the sky, in long streaks stacked down toward the hills. Add a few small streaks in the upper left and one long band low across the whole width.
lay-clouds.leave: Leave the blue showing between the streaks and through their edges, especially across the upper left of the sky.
lay-clouds.stop: Soft gold streaks cross the sky, thickest on the right half, with blue peeking through. If one goes on solid, your brush is too loaded: wipe it drier and keep the next streaks lighter.

light-clouds.first: Let the gold streaks dry first.
light-clouds.start: Start at the left edge on the lowest cloud band, with only the tip of the brush in Cream gold. That band's top is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge.
light-clouds.strokes: Skim lightly left and right along the top edge of each streak, letting the paint break up over the canvas texture.
light-clouds.inside: Most of the cream goes on the left half of the sky, over the low band and along the top of the sky. The streaks near the right edge of the canvas get only small touches on their tops.
light-clouds.leave: Leave the warm gold showing under every cream touch, and the blue between the streaks.
light-clouds.stop: The clouds have pale, glowing tops over warm gold undersides. Stop while it still looks broken and see-through, before any of it turns into a solid cream patch.

lay-hills.first: The sky must be dry so the hills get a clean top edge.
lay-hills.start: Start at the left edge with Pale violet on the far ridge line. Its top is about 2 1/4 in from the top edge.
lay-hills.strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right, following the ridges' gentle rises and dips across to the right edge.
lay-hills.inside: Pale violet makes a thin far range along the horizon. Under it, Blue-violet lays in the nearer range, whose own ridge cuts across the pale one, and fills everything beneath.
lay-hills.leave: Leave the gold sky showing above the ridge line. Keep both colors flat, with no shading.
lay-hills.stop: Carry the Blue-violet down to about 4 3/4 in from the top edge, past where the green hillside will start, and leave the canvas under it white. You should see two flat violet bands, the far one paler.

shade-hills.first: Let the hills dry fully before dry-brushing over them.
shade-hills.start: Start on the near range a little in from the left edge of the canvas, just under a ridge line, with only the tip of the brush in Blue-violet.
shade-hills.strokes: Skim lightly, pulling short strokes along the slope as it slants down toward the right edge of the canvas. Build the dark up in a few soft passes.
shade-hills.inside: The dark sits on the shadowed slopes of the nearer range, the faces turned away from the low sun. It runs in one long band along the ridge.
shade-hills.leave: Leave the pale far range and the lower part of the near hills as they are, so the two ranges read apart.
shade-hills.stop: A soft, broken darker band runs along the nearer slopes and reaches the right edge of the canvas. If it goes on solid, let it dry and keep the next passes lighter.

lay-loch.first: The hills must be dry so the water stays pale and clean.
lay-loch.start: Start at the right edge of the canvas, at the foot of the hills. The loch's middle is about 4 3/4 in from the top edge.
lay-loch.strokes: Keep the #6 flat level and pull short strokes away from the right edge, lifting off so the strip narrows to a point.
lay-loch.inside: Loch silver fills one thin, flat sliver of calm water, tucked under the hills and tapering to its tip. It is too small for ripples.
lay-loch.leave: Leave the blue-violet hills showing above and around the sliver.
lay-loch.stop: A thin pale strip of loch lies at the right edge, its tip about 9 3/4 in from the left edge. Keep it a sliver: beginners tend to make the water too thick.

lay-hillside.first: Let the hills and loch dry before painting against them.
lay-hillside.start: Start at the left edge of the canvas at the top of the hillside, about 3 1/2 in from the top edge, overlapping the foot of the hills.
lay-hillside.strokes: Pull long strokes left and right, keeping the brush level along the slope, so each band leans down toward the right edge of the canvas, the way the hillside's top edge slopes.
lay-hillside.inside: Lay the top of the hillside as a band just under the hills and the loch. Then carry long bands of Olive green on down to the bottom edge.
lay-hillside.leave: Leave white streaks of canvas between the lower green bands. The meadow covers them later. Don't paint over the loch.
lay-hillside.stop: Olive green runs from under the hills to the bottom edge in slanting bands, with bare streaks between them. Check that the hillside's top edge slopes down, not straight across.

patch-hillside.first: Let the lighter green coat from step 7 dry first, or the dark will smear into it and turn muddy.
patch-hillside.start: Begin at the top of the hillside, just under the far violet hills, at the left edge of the canvas. The first rows sit about 3 1/4 in from the top edge.
patch-hillside.strokes: Pull long, level strokes left and right across the hillside. Lay short rows of dark patches one under another, following the slope of the hilltop.
patch-hillside.inside: Keep the patches thin and close together near the hills, and wider and longer lower down. They are the dips in the rolling ground, so the land seems to roll back.
patch-hillside.leave: Leave the lighter green from step 7 showing between every row, about as much light as dark. Keep the dark off the far violet hills and the loch.
patch-hillside.stop: Stop when the dark rows reach the bottom edge of the canvas and the whole hillside reads as rolling bands. Don't make every patch the same length, or it turns into stripes.

highland-cow.note: These didn't square: step 1's facts say the paint reaches the bottom edge, but its picture stops about 3 1/4 in down. In step 3, the plan puts more cream on the right, while the change picture and facts put most on the left. Step 5's Where area is a 1/2 in box, which doesn't match its long band. Step 7's plan calls for a flat even coat, but the picture shows slanting bands with bare gaps.

blend-mist.start: Start in the sky's upper left corner with a little Pale gold. Then work Haze blue across the middle, and Deep haze blue down the right side of the canvas.
blend-mist.strokes: Make short criss-cross X strokes, overlapping them as you move across. While it's still wet, go back over it with lighter, longer side-to-side strokes to soften the joins between the colours.
blend-mist.inside: Keep the gold faint and only in the upper left corner, where the hazy sun glows. The blue gets deeper toward the right edge, where the fog is thicker and farther from the light.
blend-mist.leave: Leave the white canvas below the mist bare. The mist stops in a soft wavy line, highest on the left side of the canvas, about 6 1/4 in from the top edge.
blend-mist.stop: The upper canvas is one soft misty blend reaching the left, right and top edges, lowest on the right side of the canvas, about 3 3/4 in from the bottom edge. Don't scrub it into one flat gray.

dab-dark-wood.first: Let the mist from step 1 dry completely, or the dark will smear into it.
dab-dark-wood.start: Start along the ragged top of the dark wood, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge, and work toward the right edge.
dab-dark-wood.strokes: Dip only the brush tip, with no water, and skim lightly in short broken strokes like clumps of far trees. Build it up in several light passes; if it goes on solid, wipe the brush.
dab-dark-wood.inside: The mass is fullest and darkest low down and toward the right edge, where the wood is deepest. Its top and left side break into ragged clumps, with a small dab or two higher in the fog.
dab-dark-wood.leave: Leave the misty blend showing through the ragged top and the left side of the dark wood, and everything left of the dark wood untouched.
dab-dark-wood.stop: A dark, soft-edged wood runs from about 10 1/2 in from the left edge to the right edge, its bottom about 7 1/2 in from the top edge. The rest is still misty.

mist-wood-edge.first: Let the dark mass from step 2 dry first.
mist-wood-edge.start: Start where the dark wood meets the fog on its left side, your first strokes about 9 in from the left edge.
mist-wood-edge.strokes: Dry-brush with just the tip loaded, skimming short broken strokes into the dark edge. Then pull a few narrow pointed treetops up above the dark wood, reaching the top edge.
mist-wood-edge.inside: This lighter paint goes only around the outside: the left side of the dark wood, its bottom down to about 8 1/2 in from the top edge, and the tall tops, because fog veils the wood's edges.
mist-wood-edge.leave: Leave the dark middle and the far right part of the dark mass from step 2 showing; that is the deepest part of the wood.
mist-wood-edge.stop: The wood fades softly into the fog on its left side, along its bottom and in its pointed tops, darkest at the far right, with no hard outline anywhere.

lay-floor.first: The misty blend and the wood must be dry before you start.
lay-floor.start: Start along the bottom edge with Rust brown, from the left edge to the right edge.
lay-floor.strokes: Stroke side to side in even, creamy strokes. Without rinsing, pick up Warm ochre and paint it above the rust, toward the fog, then stroke back over the join several times while it's wet.
lay-floor.inside: Rust brown stays in front along the bottom edge; Warm ochre fills the back nearer the fog, because the far ground is lighter in the haze. A hard line at the join needs more ochre.
lay-floor.leave: Leave the white hump of bare canvas above the floor, its left side about 1 in from the left edge, as it is: the bushes cover it later.
lay-floor.stop: The floor reaches the left, right and bottom edges, its top about 7 1/2 in from the top edge, just overlapping the mist. It reads ochre at the back, rust in front.

lay-path.first: Let the floor from step 4 dry.
lay-path.start: Start at the bottom edge, where the path is widest, its left side about 6 1/2 in from the left edge.
lay-path.strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right across the path, making each stroke shorter as you work back toward the fog.
lay-path.inside: The path narrows as it goes back to a thin strip, its top about 7 1/2 in from the top edge, just below the dark wood. Keep it smoother and lighter at the back, more textured in front.
lay-path.leave: Leave the floor showing on both sides of the path; most of the path sits in the left half of the canvas.
lay-path.stop: A plain mauve-brown path runs from the bottom edge back into the fog, wide in front and thin at the back, with slightly ragged edges and no leaves yet.

pull-far-birches.first: The mist, the dark wood and the floor must all be dry.
pull-far-birches.start: Start at the foot of the trunk left of the path, its middle about 8 in from the left edge, just above the floor.
pull-far-birches.strokes: Press the full brush width at the foot, then pull straight up, turning onto the edge and easing off so the trunk tapers. Pull this one all the way to the top edge.
pull-far-birches.inside: Then pull two thinner trunks over the dark wood, their middles about 12 in from the left edge, from near the floor up into the fog. Keep all three pale and plain: they are far away.
pull-far-birches.leave: Leave the faint misty trunks from step 1 on the left side of the canvas as they are, and the dark wood showing between the two right trunks.
pull-far-birches.stop: Three thin pale trunks stand in the fog: a tall one left of the path reaching the top edge, and two against the dark wood. No bark marks yet.

mark-far-birches.first: Let the trunks from step 6 dry, or the gray will turn muddy on them.
mark-far-birches.start: Start at the foot of the trunk left of the path, where it meets the floor, then work up its lower part, whose top is about 4 3/4 in from the top edge.
mark-far-birches.strokes: Press the full width for short marks across the trunk, lifting onto the edge so each tapers. At the foot, press wide and pull out a little onto the floor, like roots.
mark-far-birches.inside: Most of the gray fills in the lower trunks down to the floor; higher up, only small scattered dashes, because far bark is soft in the mist. Do the same on the two trunks against the dark wood.
mark-far-birches.leave: Leave plenty of the pale trunk showing between the upper marks, so the birches still read as white. Pressing hard up high is the usual mistake.
mark-far-birches.stop: Each far trunk is dark and solid near the floor, pale with a few soft gray marks above, and stands firmly on the ground.

dab-dark-undergrowth.first: Let the soft gray bark marks from step 7 and the flat orange-gold floor dry first, so your taps don't lift them.
dab-dark-undergrowth.start: Start the bank of bushes at the left edge of the canvas, its top about 4 1/4 in from the top edge, tapping Warm ochre toward the path.
dab-dark-undergrowth.strokes: Wipe the dry brush on a paper towel, then tap straight in with the tip. Build rounded bumps, tapping a spot many times to make it solid. A wet or loaded brush leaves blobs, not dots.
dab-dark-undergrowth.inside: Tap solid where the bushes sit on the floor, looser in their crown. Right of the path, tap Moss olive in a low band at the foot of the dark wood, its left end about 9 3/4 in from the left edge.
dab-dark-undergrowth.leave: Leave little gaps of misty fog in the crown of the left bushes. Keep the path into the fog clear, but cover the foot of each far trunk the bushes cross.
dab-dark-undergrowth.stop: Stop when a bumpy bank about 9 in wide runs from the left edge to the path, and a low dull band hugs the dark wood's foot. No bright gold yet.

birch-grove.note: Things I couldn't fully square: step 1's picture has faint pale trunks and hardly any gold; step 4 leaves a white patch of bare canvas; steps 2 and 5 show ochre flecks no listed paint makes; and step 7 fills the lower trunks solid instead of making the small marks the plan describes.

variant.note: From step 5 on, A and B have the same pictures and nearly the same words, so they share the same faults. Step 6 says haze-blue trunks with no bark, but its picture shows white trunks already carrying dark bark marks and branches. Step 19 says small pale taps, but the picture lays a big gold glow over the whole upper left. A's own problems: step 1's picture has ghost trunks and a dark ghost shape that the words never mention, and step 4 leaves a white hump of bare canvas floating in the fog until step 8. The words do explain the hump, but a beginner would still read it as a mistake.

baseline.note: B shares A's step 6 bark-before-its-step, step 19's glow that no tap makes, and step 15's hard camouflage patches where the words describe dry-brushed shading. Its opening is cleaner: step 1 covers the whole canvas as the words say and mentions the pale trunk streaks, and step 4 has no leftover white blotch. Step 1 still shows far more ready-made trees than 'a few paler streaks' explains.

ab-line-round1.note: The two lessons differ only in steps 1 to 4. B's full-canvas fog avoids A's odd white hump and matches its words a little better, so B has a slight edge. From step 5 on they are identical, and both carry the same worse faults at steps 6, 15 and 19. Under the rule that a small edge is not a preference, this is a toss-up leaning B.

baseline.note: From step 2 on, the pictures are the same as B's, so the same faults decide the scores. Step 1 already shows the far trunks, a dark squiggle and pink patches the words don't cover. blend-mist.start: Start in the upper left corner of the canvas with Pale gold, crossing short X strokes in a patch about the size of your hand.
blend-mist.strokes: Work outward in short crossing X strokes, picking up Haze blue as you move right and down, then Deep haze blue near the right edge of the canvas, crossing each color into the last while wet.
blend-mist.inside: Keep the gold to the upper left corner of the canvas, where the low sun glows through the mist. The middle is pale blue-gray, and the deepest blue runs along the right edge of the canvas.
blend-mist.leave: Carry the blend down to about 7 3/4 in from the top edge, letting its lower edge go soft and wavy. Leave the white canvas under that line bare, because the forest floor covers it later.
blend-mist.stop: The upper canvas reads as one soft fog with no hard lines between colors. Smooth the criss-cross marks with a few long, light side-to-side strokes while wet. Don't let a stripe form where gold meets blue.

dab-dark-wood.first: Let the misty blend from step 1 dry completely, so the dry brush skims over it instead of mixing in.
dab-dark-wood.start: Start at the right edge of the canvas, about 5 1/4 in from the top edge, which is the wood's thick middle. Put only the tip of the dry brush in the paint.
dab-dark-wood.strokes: Skim short, light, upright strokes in several passes, working up and leftward like clumps of far treetops. Let the top go ragged in little bumps.
dab-dark-wood.inside: Most of the paint goes on the wood's right side and low down, thickest at its bottom. Toward its left side, about 10 1/2 in from the left edge, it thins and breaks up where the fog eats into it.
dab-dark-wood.leave: Leave the fog showing through gaps along the ragged top and the left side of the wood, and keep the bare canvas under the wood untouched. Add one small lone dab higher up in the fog, as a distant treetop.
dab-dark-wood.stop: Stop when the wood is a soft dark mass about 5 1/2 in wide, its top about 2 3/4 in from the top edge, feathery and never solid. If it starts going on solid, put less paint on the brush tip.

mist-wood-edge.first: Let the dark wood from step 2 dry completely, or this lighter paint will mix into it and turn muddy.
mist-wood-edge.start: Start at the wood's ragged left side, skimming the dry brush tip from the fog into the dark. The mist reaches out to about 9 in from the left edge.
mist-wood-edge.strokes: Skim short, light, upright strokes along the wood's left side and down its bottom. Then pull a crown of taller pointed treetops up behind the dark mass, reaching the top edge of the canvas.
mist-wood-edge.inside: The paint goes around the dark mass, not on its heart. It makes a misty fringe on the wood's left side and bottom, plus pale far treetops rising behind it, because farther trees sink into the fog.
mist-wood-edge.leave: Leave the darkest dark showing toward the right edge of the canvas, and let fog show through every broken mark. Let the ragged bottom fringe reach about 8 1/2 in from the top edge, no lower.
mist-wood-edge.stop: Stop when the wood melts into the fog on its left side and bottom, soft pale treetops rise to the top edge, and it stays darkest at the right edge. Don't cover the dark heart from step 2.

lay-floor.first: Let the fog and the dark wood dry first, because the floor is painted right up against them.
lay-floor.start: Start along the bottom edge of the canvas with the rust brown.
lay-floor.strokes: Stroke side to side, from edge to edge. Without rinsing, take the warm ochre and paint from the rust band up to the fog's ragged bottom. Then stroke back over the join several times.
lay-floor.inside: Keep the rust brown along the bottom edge and the warm ochre at the back by the fog. The far floor is paler in the mist, and the near floor is darker.
lay-floor.leave: Keep the fog, the dark wood on the right and the pale trunks clean, but cover all the white canvas in the floor.
lay-floor.stop: The floor reaches the left, right and bottom edges, and its top is about 7 1/4 in from the top edge, with the ochre melting into the rust. If you see a hard line between them, add more ochre there and blend again.
